problem_statement: timlrx/tailwind-nextjs-starter-blog is a Next.js 15 App Router blog built with Tailwind CSS and Contentlayer/MDX. The /blog collection index is rendered by layouts/ListLayoutWithTags.tsx (a client component). A recent change added an interactive Topic Browser to the top of the collection index: a row of topic chips (All / Guides / Releases / Essays / Engineering) above a stream of post cards, plus a live count readout that reads 'Showing all 10 posts' and, once a topic is picked, 'Showing N of 10 . <Topic>'. Clicking a chip is meant to filter the post cards to that topic and re-sync the readout. The same change added a shared 'Keep reading' rail (components/ReadingRail.tsx) that carries the reader between the collection, the current topic hub and the latest posts, and is meant to appear on the /blog index, every /tags/<tag> hub and every /blog/<slug> article. The feature shipped with four defects that a QA pass must complete: (1) clicking a topic chip moves the active chip but the card grid and count readout stay frozen at the initial 'Showing all 10 posts' view, so the filter never actually narrows the collection; (2) the Keep-reading rail is wired only on the /blog index, so it silently disappears on the topic hubs and article pages; (3) on a 390px phone the chip row is pinned to a fixed over-wide non-wrapping line so the /blog document scrolls sideways; and (4) the Topic Browser panel is visually broken - the chips collide and shingle over one another with clipped text, the selected chip is rendered dark-text-on-dark-fill (illegible), the count readout is pale-grey 9px (unreadable) and the post cards overlap and clip off the right edge. Complete the Topic Browser so the topic chips actually filter the post cards and re-sync the 'Showing N of 10 . <Topic>' readout, so the shared Keep-reading rail renders on the /blog index, the /tags/<tag> hubs and the /blog/<slug> articles alike, so the chip row reflows to fit a 390px phone with no horizontal overflow, and so the panel lays out cleanly and legibly on desktop and tablet - while leaving all post copy, tag lists, the author panel, the previous/next-article footer, the Back-to-the-blog link, and the Blog/Tags/Projects/About header navigation unchanged.
required_content: On the /blog collection index, clicking a Topic Browser chip filters the post cards to that topic and updates the count readout: clicking Guides shows exactly the 3 Guides posts and the readout reads 'Showing 3 of 10 . Guides'; clicking Releases shows 3 posts and reads 'Showing 3 of 10 . Releases'.

The shared 'Keep reading' rail renders on the /blog index, on every /tags/<tag> hub, and on every /blog/<slug> article page, so the cross-page reading continuity surface is present on all three route families.
On a 390px mobile viewport the /blog collection index has no horizontal overflow beyond a small tolerance: the Topic Browser chip row wraps or reflows to fit.

On desktop (1440px) and tablet (834px) the Topic Browser panel lays out cleanly with legible chips, a legible selected chip, a readable count readout, and post cards that do not overlap or clip, with no horizontal overflow and no visual regression.

The post copy, the Tags lists, the author panel, the Previous/Next-article footer links, the Back-to-the-blog link, and the Blog/Tags/Projects/About header navigation remain present and unchanged in content and structure. No new console errors or failed network requests are introduced; the blog continues to serve as a self-contained static Next.js export with locally served assets.
design_constraints: Preserve the TailwindBlog editorial design language: gray borders, primary-accent text, white/dark surfaces, compact typography, and the existing collection-index structure and reading order.

Complete ONLY the Topic Browser filter wiring, the Keep-reading rail's cross-route presence, and the Topic Browser panel layout; do not rewrite post copy, change the topic set or chip labels, or change the header navigation.
The layout fix must live in the Topic Browser's own stylesheet (css/topic-browser.css) and must not depend on hiding overflow at the body/html level or clipping content off-screen to mask the spill.
The Topic Browser must fit 390px mobile, 834px tablet, and 1440px desktop viewports; all chips must remain readable and clickable and the selected chip must be legible at every size.
Keep the Next.js App Router build pipeline intact - the static export must still emit a working /blog index, /blog/<slug> article layout and /tags/<tag> routes.
state_constraints: desktop_blog captures the /blog collection index at 1440px with the Topic Browser panel and the Keep-reading rail scrolled into view; the panel and cards lay out cleanly with no horizontal overflow.
mobile_blog captures the /blog index at 390px: with the defect the chip row forces the document wider than the viewport; the completed responsive layout brings horizontal overflow within tolerance.
tablet_blog captures /blog at 834px, where the panel already fits and must continue to fit.
desktop_blog_guides clicks the Guides chip: the readout must change to 'Showing 3 of 10 . Guides' and the grid must show exactly the Guides posts.
desktop_blog_releases clicks the Releases chip: the readout must change to 'Showing 3 of 10 . Releases'.
mobile_blog_component captures the Topic Browser panel at 390px, where the completed layout is legible and overflow-free.
desktop_tag loads /tags/writings at 1440px and must render the shared Keep-reading rail.
desktop_post loads /blog/the-time-machine at 1440px and must render the shared Keep-reading rail, the tag list, the previous/next footer and the Back-to-the-blog link.
desktop_about captures /about at 1440px, confirming a route without the Topic Browser is unaffected.

change_completion: Clicking a Topic Browser chip filters the post cards and re-syncs the count readout to 'Showing N of 10 . <Topic>' (Guides -> 3, Releases -> 3).
The shared Keep-reading rail renders on the /blog index, the /tags/<tag> hubs and the /blog/<slug> article pages.
The mobile /blog index no longer overflows horizontally: the chip row reflows to fit a 390px viewport.
design_consistency: The completed Topic Browser preserves the TailwindBlog editorial identity, the collection-index copy, and all surrounding content.

The panel is legible: chips do not collide, the selected chip is readable, the count readout is readable, and the post cards do not overlap or clip; the fix does not clip or hide content to mask overflow.
responsive: At 390px the Topic Browser chip row wraps or flexes down so the document width stays within the viewport.
At 834px and 1440px the panel lays out cleanly with no horizontal overflow.
regression: The post copy, author panel, Tags lists, Previous/Next-article footer, Back-to-the-blog link, and header navigation remain present and unchanged.
No new console errors or failed network requests appear on any captured state.

author_notes: Repo-grounded extend_interaction/regression_continuity/cross_page task on the timlrx tailwind-nextjs-starter-blog template (Next.js 15 App Router + Tailwind + Contentlayer/MDX, built as a static export and served with a static file server). The native lever is the /blog collection index's own Topic Browser: a topic-chip filter that filters the repo's real 10 MDX post cards and reports a 'Showing N of 10 . <Topic>' count, hosted in the repo's ListLayoutWithTags client component. A shared Keep-reading rail is a cross-route feature across the collection, tag hubs and article pages. Four orthogonal gates carry difficulty: the topic filter re-syncs its readout (interaction_assertions), the rail is present on the tag and post routes (cross-route dom_assertions), the chip row wraps on a 390px phone (no_horizontal_overflow, tolerance 24px), and the panel stays legible and uncollided (visual_regression pixelmatch/ssim/block_fidelity). The reference completes all four; the baseline is the original defect (broken/overflowing panel and blog-only rail) with the filter wiring already correct, so it passes only the interaction gate; the bad solution additionally freezes the readout so it fails all four. The design language (gray borders, primary-accent chips, white/dark surfaces) and the topic buckets are drawn from the repo's actual posts. This task lives on the collection index and drives the reading finder; it is distinct from a post-layout reading strip.
